question: How do Class A performance rules treat engine failure?

options.text: It is assumed only during the cruise
It is not considered for take-off
It is assumed only above 300 ft
It must be considered in every phase of flight

explanation: For Class A aeroplanes engine failure must be accounted for at all stages of flight, which brings in many new speeds and concepts.

question: Which three take-off distance conditions must a Class A aeroplane meet?

options.text: ASDR ≤ TODA and TODR ≤ ASDA, with TORR ignored
Each required distance ≤ its available one

explanation: The accelerate-stop distance, take-off distance and take-off run required must each be within the matching available distance, using a single V1.

question: Which of these is a limit on Class A take-off mass?
explanation: The limits are field length, climb, obstacle clearance, brake energy, tyre speed, runway strength and the maximum structural mass.

question: With all engines operating, how is the net take-off run required (with a clearway) found?

options.text: Distance to VLOF plus half the airborne distance to 35 ft, × 1.25

explanation: The all-engines TORR is the distance to VLOF plus half the distance from VLOF to 35 ft, all multiplied by 1.15.

question: With one engine inoperative on a dry runway, where does the take-off run required end?
explanation: With the critical engine failed on a dry runway, the TORR ends at a point equidistant between VLOF and the point where 35 ft is reached. This one is not factored.

question: With one engine inoperative on a wet runway, where do the take-off run and distance end?
explanation: On a wet runway the one-engine distance is taken to 15 ft, flown so that V2 is reached by 35 ft. The lower screen reduces the mass penalty of a wet runway.

question: The all-engines distance to the midpoint between VLOF and 35 ft is 1 700 m. The one-engine dry figure is 1 900 m and the one-engine wet figure 1 940 m. What is the net TORR?
explanation: All engines: 1 700 × 1.15 = 1 955 m. The greatest of 1 955, 1 900 and 1 940 is 1 955 m.

question: How is the all-engines take-off distance required found?
explanation: The all-engines TODR is the horizontal distance to 35 ft multiplied by 1.15. The one-engine distances are not factored.

question: How many cases make up the take-off distance required, and which is used?

options.text: Three cases; the average is used
Two cases; the smaller of the two is used

explanation: TODR is the greatest of: all engines to 35 ft × 1.15; one engine to 35 ft on a dry runway; and one engine to 15 ft on a wet runway.

question: What time allowance is added to the wet accelerate-stop distance?

options.text: A distance equal to 2 seconds at VR
A distance equal to 1 second at V1
A distance equal to 2 seconds at V1

explanation: The wet accelerate-stop cases add a distance equivalent to 2 seconds at the wet-runway V1.

question: Which cases make up the accelerate-stop distance required on a wet runway?

options.text: One engine failed at V1 only, with 2 seconds added
AEO, OEI and the dry ASD

explanation: The wet ASDR is the greatest of: all-engines acceleration to V1 then stop on a wet surface; engine failure at VEF then stop; and the dry accelerate-stop distance.

question: What is VMCG?

options.text: The lowest airborne control speed with the critical engine failed
The lowest ground speed at which the take-off can be continued with the critical engine failed
The highest speed from which the brakes can stop the aeroplane
The lowest speed at which the aeroplane can lift off

explanation: VMCG is the minimum speed on the ground at which, with the critical engine suddenly inoperative and the others at take-off thrust, the take-off can be safely continued.

question: Why can only the rudder be used to control yaw at VMCG?

options.text: Using the ailerons on the ground could put a wing into the runway
The nose wheel steering is used instead
The ailerons are locked on the ground
The ailerons have no effect at all on yaw on the ground

explanation: On the ground ailerons cannot be used to counter the asymmetric yaw without risking a wing strike, so the rudder alone must provide control.

question: How does increasing air density affect VMCG?

options.text: It increases VMCG only on wet runways

explanation: Denser air gives more thrust from the live engine, so the yaw after a failure is stronger and a higher speed is needed for the rudder to cope.

question: What controls the value of VMCG?
explanation: VMCG depends on the asymmetric thrust, which depends on air density. Low temperature and low altitude give high density and a high VMCG.

question: Why is VEF about one second before V1?

options.text: It is the time for V1 to be called
The pilot needs time to recognise the engine failure
The engine takes one second to spool down after the failure
The brakes take one second to apply

explanation: About one second is needed to recognise a failure, so for it to be recognised at V1 the engine must fail at VEF, just before V1.

question: What is the lowest value V1 may have?
explanation: V1 may not be less than VEF plus the speed gained during recognition, and must not be less than VMCG.

question: What are the upper limits on V1?

options.text: It must not exceed VMCG or VEF
It must not exceed V2 or VFTO
It must not exceed VR or VMBE

explanation: V1 must not be greater than VR or VMBE, and must not be less than VMCG.

question: Why must V1 not be less than VMCG?

options.text: Below VMCG the aeroplane cannot rotate
Control would be lost if it continued
Below VMCG the brakes would overheat
Below VMCG the tyres would exceed their speed limit on the runway

explanation: V1 is a speed from which the take-off can be continued after a failure, which is impossible if the aeroplane is uncontrollable on the ground.

question: Why must V1 not exceed VMBE?

options.text: Above VMBE the brakes could not stop the aeroplane safely
Above VMBE directional control would be lost on the ground
Above VMBE the aeroplane would lift off
Above VMBE the tyres would burst

explanation: V1 must be a speed from which a stop is possible; above VMBE the brakes cannot absorb the energy, however much runway remains.

question: On the graph of distance required against engine failure speed, where is the balanced V1?

options.text: Where the ASDR is greatest on the graph

explanation: At the intersection the take-off distance required equals the accelerate-stop distance required, giving the least total field length.

question: V1 is increased above the balanced value. What happens to ASDR, TODR and field length required?

options.text: ASDR decreases, TODR increases, field length required increases
ASDR increases, TODR decreases, field length required is unchanged
Both decrease; field length required decreases
ASDR increases, TODR decreases, field length required increases

explanation: A later failure speed means a longer stop but a shorter continued take-off. Away from the balanced point the required field length always increases.

question: V1 is reduced below the balanced value. What happens to ASDR and TODR?
explanation: An earlier decision means a shorter stop but a longer continued take-off on one engine; the field length required increases.

question: How does increasing the take-off mass affect V1?

options.text: It decreases on dry runways only

explanation: A heavier aeroplane needs higher take-off speeds, so V1 increases.

question: How does a larger take-off flap setting affect V1 and VR for the same mass?
explanation: More flap lowers the stall speed and take-off speeds, so V1 and VR decrease.

question: How does decreasing air density affect V1 and VR?
explanation: Lower density (higher temperature or altitude) gives higher V1 and VR in the speed tables.

question: How do an upslope and a headwind affect V1?

options.text: An upslope increases it; a headwind decreases it

explanation: Upslopes and headwinds increase V1; downslopes and tailwinds reduce it.

question: What is VMBE?

options.text: The speed at which the brakes are released
The top speed the brakes can stop from
The speed limited by tyre heating
The lowest speed at which full braking is allowed on a dry runway

explanation: VMBE is the maximum brake energy speed: if the take-off is rejected above it, the brakes cannot stop the aeroplane safely, whatever the runway left.

question: Which variables affect VMBE?
explanation: Brake energy depends on the true ground speed and mass, so VMBE varies with pressure altitude, temperature, mass, slope and wind.

question: How does a heavier take-off mass affect VMBE?

options.text: It increases VMBE on a downslope

explanation: The energy to absorb is ½MV²; with more mass, the brakes reach their limit at a lower speed.

question: The balanced V1 is below VMCG. What can be done?

options.text: Raise V1 to VMCG, accepting a longer field length
Lower VMCG by using more thrust from both engines

explanation: V1 can be increased until it equals VMCG; ASDR then increases and TODR decreases. If the runway is long enough, this is acceptable.

question: What is VMU?

options.text: The highest speed for tyre safety
The speed at which rotation begins
The minimum control speed in the air with one engine
The lowest speed at which the aeroplane can safely lift off and continue

explanation: VMU is the minimum unstick speed. It is not used operationally because control is poor so close to the stall.

question: How can an aeroplane lift off at VMU with lift less than weight?

options.text: The ground effect doubles the lift
The high nose attitude gives a vertical component of thrust

explanation: At a high enough nose attitude, part of the thrust acts upwards and, with lift, balances weight. The attitude may be limited by elevator power or tail strike.

question: Which of these limits must VR satisfy?

options.text: Not less than V2 and not less than the brake energy speed VMBE

explanation: VR may not be less than V1, 1.05 VMCA, a speed that lets V2 be reached by 35 ft, or a speed giving a safe VLOF margin over VMU.

question: With all engines operating and the aeroplane not geometry-limited, what is the minimum VLOF relative to VMU?
explanation: VLOF must be at least 110% of VMU with all engines and 105% with one engine inoperative. If geometry-limited, the figures are 108% and 104%.

question: If VMU is limited by tail contact with the runway, what is the minimum one-engine-inoperative VLOF?
explanation: For geometry-limited aeroplanes the margins are 108% (all engines) and 104% (one engine inoperative).

question: What happens if the aeroplane is rotated to the correct attitude but too early?

options.text: It cannot lift off at all
It lifts off earlier, so the take-off distance is shortened

explanation: The aeroplane will not lift off until the normal VLOF, but the extra drag while rotated adds distance.

question: Why is it vital that leading edge devices are set for take-off?

options.text: They shorten the accelerate-stop distance after a reject

explanation: Rotating beyond the normal attitude can bring the wing close to its stalling angle near the ground; correctly set leading edge devices prevent a ground stall.

question: What does certification require about rotating 5 kt below VR?

options.text: The TOD must not exceed the normal one
It must be impossible to lift off
The take-off distance may increase by up to 10% compared with VR
It must lead to a tail strike warning

explanation: The take-off distance with rotation 5 kt early must not exceed the distance using the established VR. Reasonable variations must not markedly increase the distance (more than 1%).

question: What is the minimum V2 (V2MIN) for a twin-engine jet without special stall-reducing provisions?

options.text: The greater of 1.2 VSR and 1.05 VMCA
The greater of 1.08 VSR and 1.1 VMCA
The greater of 1.13 VSR and 1.1 VMCA

explanation: V2MIN is not less than 1.13 VSR for twin and three-engine turboprops and turbojets without a means of significantly reducing the one-engine power-on stall speed, and not less than 1.1 VMCA.

question: For which aeroplanes may V2MIN be as low as 1.08 VSR?

options.text: Four-engine turboprops and specially fitted jets
Aeroplanes with leading edge slats but no trailing edge flaps

explanation: The 1.08 VSR factor applies to turboprops with more than three engines and turbojets with provision for significantly reducing the one-engine power-on stall speed.

question: Which two conditions set the minimum V2?

options.text: V2MIN and VR + increment to 35 ft

explanation: V2 must be no less than V2MIN and no less than VR plus the increment gained before reaching 35 ft.

question: After an engine failure on take-off, up to what height is V2 flown?
explanation: V2 is held until 400 ft, the point where acceleration and flap retraction may begin.

question: Why is V2 called the take-off safety speed?

options.text: It is the speed below which a stop is always possible on any runway
It is the maximum speed for flap extension
It is the speed for the steepest climb on all engines
It is safely above stall and VMCA and gives the required climb

explanation: V2 is the slowest speed giving enough excess thrust for the required one-engine climb, with margins over the stall and minimum control speeds.

question: What is V3?

options.text: The speed at which flap retraction ends

explanation: V3 is the steady initial climb speed with all engines operating, faster than V2.

question: What typically limits the maximum tyre speed of a jet airliner?

options.text: The strength of the wheel bolts
The air pressure in the brake system
Heat from the speed and load on the tyre

explanation: Rolling generates heat that rises with speed and load; too much can destroy the tyre or over-pressurise it, though fusible plugs help.

question: At what point in the take-off is the tyre speed highest?

options.text: At the end of a rejected take-off

explanation: The highest ground speed the tyres see is at lift-off, so tyre speed limits are set at or above the fastest VLOF.

question: How does a tailwind affect the tyre-speed-limited take-off mass?

options.text: It increases it at high altitude

explanation: A tailwind increases the ground speed at VLOF, so a lower mass (lower VLOF) is needed to stay within the tyre limit.

question: For which speed is brake energy calculated?
explanation: Kinetic energy is ½MV² with V the true ground speed, so the IAS equivalent of VMBE changes with altitude, temperature and wind.

question: Why can runway slope affect VMBE?

options.text: Slope changes the effective mass of the aeroplane on the runway
Height change adds or removes energy

explanation: Stopping on a downslope means the brakes must also absorb potential energy, reducing VMBE; an upslope helps.

question: V1 exceeds VMBE. What must be done?

options.text: Use a higher thrust setting to shorten the take-off

explanation: The mass must be reduced; the flight manual gives the mass reduction per knot by which V1 exceeds VMBE.

question: Why may a rejected take-off soon after landing be dangerous for the brakes?

options.text: The brakes are already hot and can absorb less energy
The brakes are colder than normal
The tyres are under-inflated after a landing and a long taxi
The anti-skid is switched off after landing

explanation: VMBE assumes brakes at ambient temperature. After a recent landing or long taxi they are hot, so the flight manual gives a required cooling time.

question: How is a runway's bearing strength compared with the aeroplane for normal operations?

options.text: The aeroplane's mass must not exceed the pavement number in tonnes
The pavement's number must not exceed the aeroplane's
The aeroplane's classification number must not exceed the pavement's
Only the tyre pressure is compared

explanation: The pavement classification number is compared with the aircraft classification number; normal operation is allowed if the aircraft's number does not exceed the pavement's.

question: When does an aerodrome have a balanced field?

options.text: When there is a stopway at both ends

explanation: A balanced field has equal take-off distance and accelerate-stop distance available. A runway with no stopway or clearway is balanced.

question: What does the balanced field length required represent?

options.text: The shortest distance for an all-engines take-off with no failure
Enough to stop or go at any failure speed
The distance needed to reach V1
The runway length minus the stopway

explanation: It is the length where TODR equals ASDR; whatever the failure speed, the distance is enough to stop before V1 or continue after it.

question: At low weight and altitude, the balanced V1 is below VMCG. What happens to the field length required?

options.text: It equals the balanced field length
It equals the TODR at VMCG
It equals the ASDR at VMCG

explanation: V1 is raised to VMCG, so TODR is less and ASDR more than the balanced value; the field length needed is the ASDR at VMCG.

question: In hot and high conditions at high mass, the balanced V1 exceeds VMBE. What happens to the field length required?

options.text: It equals the balanced field length
It equals the TODR at VMBE
It equals the ASDR at VMBE

explanation: V1 is reduced to VMBE, giving a longer TODR and a shorter ASDR; the field length is the TODR at VMBE.

question: An aeroplane with very good brakes has a balanced V1 above VR. What is done?

options.text: VR is reduced to the balanced V1 so that they match
V1 = VR; field = TODR at VR

explanation: V1 must not exceed VR, so it is set equal to VR and the field length required is the TODR at that speed.

question: When the field available is longer than the balanced field required, what can be done with V1?

options.text: It must equal VR on every runway

explanation: There is then a range of acceptable V1 values, from VGO (lowest for a continued take-off) to VSTOP (highest for a stop).

question: How can balanced field data be used at an aerodrome that is not balanced?

options.text: Assume a balanced field equal to the lesser of TODA and ASDA
Use TODA plus ASDA divided by two
Assume a balanced field equal to the greater of TODA and ASDA

explanation: The lesser of TODA and ASDA is taken as the balanced field. The resulting mass is conservative but is often enough.

question: How does Class A take-off data usually present its results, compared with Class B?

options.text: As a time to reach V1
As a maximum mass for the runway available
As a percentage of the runway used
As a distance for a given mass

explanation: Class B charts give the distance for a mass; Class A charts usually give the maximum mass for the runway, which suits an airline wanting the most payload.

question: Which runway length is entered on a balanced-field field-limit graph that does not account for stopway or clearway?
explanation: The graph assumes TORA, TODA and ASDA are the same, so only the TORA is entered. Stopway or clearway is handled separately by V1 corrections.

question: What is the field limit mass?

options.text: The greatest mass that still meets the climb gradients
The mass at which V1 equals VR
The most mass the runway allows

explanation: The field limit brake release mass is the maximum mass at which the TORR, TODR and ASDR remain within the distances available.

question: What is the climb limit mass also called?
explanation: The climb-limited mass depends on weight (mass), altitude and temperature, so it is called the WAT or MAT limit.

question: Which climb gradient does the climb limit mass of a twin ensure?
explanation: The climb limit mass guarantees the most severe gradient requirement, the second segment, which is 2.4% for a twin.

question: Why is there no wind correction on the climb limit mass chart?

options.text: The wind correction is applied to V2 instead
The climb gradients are air gradients
The chart assumes a 10 kt headwind
Wind is always assumed to be zero for Class A

explanation: The regulatory climb gradients are measured through the air, so wind does not affect them.

question: What is the performance-limited take-off mass?

options.text: The highest of the performance limits
The lower of the field and climb limits only, ignoring tyres
The lowest of the field, climb, obstacle, tyre and brake energy limits

explanation: The performance-limited mass is the lowest of all the performance limits for the day.

question: What is the regulated take-off mass?

options.text: The performance-limited mass plus the start and taxi fuel
The lower of performance and structural limits

explanation: The regulated take-off mass is the lower of the performance-limited take-off mass and the maximum structural take-off mass.

question: Field limit 63 500 kg, climb limit 61 200 kg, tyre limit 66 000 kg, brake energy limit 64 000 kg, maximum structural take-off mass 62 800 kg. What is the regulated take-off mass?
explanation: The performance-limited mass is the lowest performance value, 61 200 kg (climb). It is below the 62 800 kg structural limit, so it is the regulated take-off mass.

subtopic: Speeds and settings for the take-off
question: Once the regulated take-off mass is known, what is found next?

options.text: The landing distance at the destination

explanation: The V1, VR and V2 for the mass, and the take-off thrust (% N1), are then found from the tables.

subtopic: Speeds and settings for the take-off
question: The tabulated V1 is 138 kt at 55 000 kg and 145 kt at 60 000 kg. What is V1 at 57 000 kg, before corrections?

subtopic: Speeds and settings for the take-off
question: Take-off speed tables are usually based on a balanced field. What must be done if the take-off mass used stopway or clearway?

options.text: Use the tables unchanged, as for any runway

explanation: The tabulated speeds assume TORA = TODA = ASDA; if stopway or clearway was used, V1 is adjusted from the manual's table.

subtopic: Speeds and settings for the take-off
question: After finding V1 for the regulated mass, which two speeds must it be checked against?
explanation: V1 must not be below VMCG or above VMBE, so both are checked for the day's conditions.

subtopic: Speeds and settings for the take-off
question: On what does the take-off stabiliser trim setting mainly depend?

options.text: The planned cruise altitude for the flight

explanation: The stabiliser trim for take-off is read from a table using the CG and the take-off mass (and flap setting).
